--- title: "Data wrangling II" subtitle: "POL51" author: "Haley Daarstad" institute: "University of California, Davis" date: today date-format: long format: revealjs: chalkboard: true slide-number: true height: 900 width: 1600 code-line-numbers: true smooth-scrawl: true theme: [simple, html/custom.scss] incremental: true title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: img/dubois-spiral-2.png data-background-size: contain data-background-position: right data-background-color: "#dc354a" --- # Plan for today {.center background-color="#dc354a"} Objects . . . mutate() . . . summarize() . . . Homework and midterm questions # Objects {background-color="#dc354a"} ## Objects and Pipes Step 1-2: the data, the pipe, the wrangling functions ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} apples |> filter(sweet == FALSE) ``` :::
. . . Step 3: store the subsetted data as a new **object** for later use ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} green_apples = apples |> filter(sweet == FALSE) ``` ::: ## Reminder on Objects In programming, **objects** can be used to store all sorts of stuff for later use . . . data, functions, values . . . We create objects using `=` or `<-` . . . Like this: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} new_object = stuff |> filter(year == 1999) ``` ::: . . . Or like this: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} new_object <- stuff |> filter(year == 1999) ``` ::: ## Naming objects > *There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.* -- Phil Karlton . . . Recommend: keep it short, easy to type, informative, and use `_` to separate words . . . # Making new variables with `mutate()` `mutate()` **adds** new variables to data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](img/mutate.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## Using mutate ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} murder_set ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 100 × 4 state city population murder_total 1 Alabama Mobile 248431 50.0 2 Alaska Anchorage 296188 27.0 3 Arizona Chandler 249355 5.01 4 Arizona Gilbert 242090 5.01 5 Arizona Glendale 249273 12.0 6 Arizona Mesa 492268 23.0 7 Arizona Phoenix 1608139 154. 8 Arizona Scottsdale 251840 5.01 9 Arizona Tucson 532323 46.0 10 California Anaheim 353400 10.0 # ℹ 90 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Using mutate ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} murder_set |> mutate() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 100 × 4 state city population murder_total 1 Alabama Mobile 248431 50.0 2 Alaska Anchorage 296188 27.0 3 Arizona Chandler 249355 5.01 4 Arizona Gilbert 242090 5.01 5 Arizona Glendale 249273 12.0 6 Arizona Mesa 492268 23.0 7 Arizona Phoenix 1608139 154. 8 Arizona Scottsdale 251840 5.01 9 Arizona Tucson 532323 46.0 10 California Anaheim 353400 10.0 # ℹ 90 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Using mutate ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} murder_set |> mutate(murder_capita = murder_total / population) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 100 × 5 state city population murder_total murder_capita 1 Alabama Mobile 248431 50.0 0.000201 2 Alaska Anchorage 296188 27.0 0.0000912 3 Arizona Chandler 249355 5.01 0.0000201 4 Arizona Gilbert 242090 5.01 0.0000207 5 Arizona Glendale 249273 12.0 0.0000481 6 Arizona Mesa 492268 23.0 0.0000467 7 Arizona Phoenix 1608139 154. 0.0000955 8 Arizona Scottsdale 251840 5.01 0.0000199 9 Arizona Tucson 532323 46.0 0.0000864 10 California Anaheim 353400 10.0 0.0000283 # ℹ 90 more rows ``` ::: ::: Notice that I named a new variable, `murder_capita` ## Using mutate ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} murder_set |> mutate(murder_capita = murder_total / population, murder_rate = murder_capita * 100000) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 100 × 6 state city population murder_total murder_capita murder_rate 1 Alabama Mobile 248431 50.0 0.000201 20.1 2 Alaska Anchorage 296188 27.0 0.0000912 9.12 3 Arizona Chandler 249355 5.01 0.0000201 2.01 4 Arizona Gilbert 242090 5.01 0.0000207 2.07 5 Arizona Glendale 249273 12.0 0.0000481 4.81 6 Arizona Mesa 492268 23.0 0.0000467 4.67 7 Arizona Phoenix 1608139 154. 0.0000955 9.55 8 Arizona Scottsdale 251840 5.01 0.0000199 1.99 9 Arizona Tucson 532323 46.0 0.0000864 8.64 10 California Anaheim 353400 10.0 0.0000283 2.83 # ℹ 90 more rows ``` ::: ::: Notice the new **columns** ## Forgetting to store If you don't store your changes, they will melt away, like tears in the rain ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} murder_set |> mutate(murder_capita = murder_total / population, murder_rate = murder_capita * 100000) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} murder_set ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 100 × 4 state city population murder_total 1 Alabama Mobile 248431 50.0 2 Alaska Anchorage 296188 27.0 3 Arizona Chandler 249355 5.01 4 Arizona Gilbert 242090 5.01 5 Arizona Glendale 249273 12.0 6 Arizona Mesa 492268 23.0 7 Arizona Phoenix 1608139 154. 8 Arizona Scottsdale 251840 5.01 9 Arizona Tucson 532323 46.0 10 California Anaheim 353400 10.0 # ℹ 90 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## New object, or overwite the old one? . . . You can make a new object: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} murder_rates = murder_set |> mutate(murder_capita = murder_total / population, murder_rate = murder_capita * 100000) ``` ::: . . . Or overwrite the old one ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} murder_set = murder_set |> mutate(murder_capita = murder_total / population, murder_rate = murder_capita * 100000) ``` ::: . . . In general, overwriting when you are **adding** stuff to your data (`mutate`) is fine ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} murder_set ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 100 × 6 state city population murder_total murder_capita murder_rate 1 Alabama Mobile 248431 50.0 0.000201 20.1 2 Alaska Anchorage 296188 27.0 0.0000912 9.12 3 Arizona Chandler 249355 5.01 0.0000201 2.01 4 Arizona Gilbert 242090 5.01 0.0000207 2.07 5 Arizona Glendale 249273 12.0 0.0000481 4.81 6 Arizona Mesa 492268 23.0 0.0000467 4.67 7 Arizona Phoenix 1608139 154. 0.0000955 9.55 8 Arizona Scottsdale 251840 5.01 0.0000199 1.99 9 Arizona Tucson 532323 46.0 0.0000864 8.64 10 California Anaheim 353400 10.0 0.0000283 2.83 # ℹ 90 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## New object, or overwite the old one? Overwriting when you are **removing** information from the data can be bad . . . For example, when we `filter()` . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder = gapminder |> filter(continent == "Africa") gapminder ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 624 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Algeria Africa 1952 43.1 9279525 2449. 2 Algeria Africa 1957 45.7 10270856 3014. 3 Algeria Africa 1962 48.3 11000948 2551. 4 Algeria Africa 1967 51.4 12760499 3247. 5 Algeria Africa 1972 54.5 14760787 4183. 6 Algeria Africa 1977 58.0 17152804 4910. 7 Algeria Africa 1982 61.4 20033753 5745. 8 Algeria Africa 1987 65.8 23254956 5681. 9 Algeria Africa 1992 67.7 26298373 5023. 10 Algeria Africa 1997 69.2 29072015 4797. # ℹ 614 more rows ``` ::: ::: . . . This is bad, since we lose the original `gapminder` data # Creating categories ## Creating categories with `case_when()` . . . Sometimes we want to create **categorical variables** (tall, short, poor, rich, Republican-leaning, Democrat-leaning, etc.) . . . We can use `case_when()`, which goes **within** `mutate()` . . . Like `filter()`, `case_when()` also relies on logical operators ## Who won the county? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
sample from elections dataset
name state per_gop_2020 per_dem_2020
Tipton County TN 0.73 0.25
New Haven County CT 0.41 0.58
Pawnee County NE 0.75 0.23
Franklin County AR 0.80 0.18
Dickinson County MI 0.66 0.33
Freeborn County MN 0.57 0.41
Hardin County OH 0.75 0.23
Tuscola County MI 0.69 0.30
Los Alamos County NM 0.35 0.61
San Francisco County CA 0.13 0.85
````` ::: ::: ## Who won the county? The general formula: `case_when(CONDITION ~ LABEL)` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} small_elections ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,152 × 4 name state per_gop_2020 per_dem_2020 1 Autauga County AL 0.714 0.270 2 Baldwin County AL 0.762 0.224 3 Barbour County AL 0.535 0.458 4 Bibb County AL 0.784 0.207 5 Blount County AL 0.896 0.0957 6 Bullock County AL 0.248 0.747 7 Butler County AL 0.575 0.418 8 Calhoun County AL 0.688 0.298 9 Chambers County AL 0.573 0.416 10 Cherokee County AL 0.860 0.132 # ℹ 3,142 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Who won the county? The general formula: `case_when(CONDITION ~ LABEL)` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} small_elections |> mutate(who_won = case_when(per_gop_2020 > per_dem_2020 ~ "Republicans")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,152 × 5 name state per_gop_2020 per_dem_2020 who_won 1 Autauga County AL 0.714 0.270 Republicans 2 Baldwin County AL 0.762 0.224 Republicans 3 Barbour County AL 0.535 0.458 Republicans 4 Bibb County AL 0.784 0.207 Republicans 5 Blount County AL 0.896 0.0957 Republicans 6 Bullock County AL 0.248 0.747 7 Butler County AL 0.575 0.418 Republicans 8 Calhoun County AL 0.688 0.298 Republicans 9 Chambers County AL 0.573 0.416 Republicans 10 Cherokee County AL 0.860 0.132 Republicans # ℹ 3,142 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: callout-note Remember when we `mutate()` we have to name the new variable ::: ::: notes point out the NA ::: ## Who won the county? The general formula: `case_when(CONDITION ~ LABEL)` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} small_elections |> mutate(who_won = case_when(per_gop_2020 > per_dem_2020 ~ "Republicans", per_dem_2020 > per_gop_2020 ~ "Democrats")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3,152 × 5 name state per_gop_2020 per_dem_2020 who_won 1 Autauga County AL 0.714 0.270 Republicans 2 Baldwin County AL 0.762 0.224 Republicans 3 Barbour County AL 0.535 0.458 Republicans 4 Bibb County AL 0.784 0.207 Republicans 5 Blount County AL 0.896 0.0957 Republicans 6 Bullock County AL 0.248 0.747 Democrats 7 Butler County AL 0.575 0.418 Republicans 8 Calhoun County AL 0.688 0.298 Republicans 9 Chambers County AL 0.573 0.416 Republicans 10 Cherokee County AL 0.860 0.132 Republicans # ℹ 3,142 more rows ``` ::: ::: # Summarizing data in R {background-color="#dc354a"} ## Summary statistics with `summarize()` We can use `summarize()` to **calculate** things like the mean, median, etc. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](img/summarize.png){fig-align='center' width=50%} ::: ::: . . . Summarizing **condenses** data into statistics ## Using `summarize()` Say I want to know the average life expectancy in the world in 2007: . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder %>% filter(year == 2007) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 52 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Algeria Africa 2007 72.3 33333216 6223. 2 Angola Africa 2007 42.7 12420476 4797. 3 Benin Africa 2007 56.7 8078314 1441. 4 Botswana Africa 2007 50.7 1639131 12570. 5 Burkina Faso Africa 2007 52.3 14326203 1217. 6 Burundi Africa 2007 49.6 8390505 430. 7 Cameroon Africa 2007 50.4 17696293 2042. 8 Central African Republic Africa 2007 44.7 4369038 706. 9 Chad Africa 2007 50.7 10238807 1704. 10 Comoros Africa 2007 65.2 710960 986. # ℹ 42 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## Using `summarize()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder %>% filter(year == 2007) %>% summarize() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 0 ``` ::: ::: ## Using `summarize()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder %>% filter(year == 2007) %>% summarize(avg_life = mean(lifeExp)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 avg_life 1 54.8 ``` ::: ::: Notice how the data has been *summarized*: only one row . . . Notice that I've *named* the summary statistic `avg_life` ## Using `summarize()` What if I also wanted to know the **median** life expectancy? . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder %>% filter(year == 2007) %>% summarize(avg_life = mean(lifeExp), med_life = median(lifeExp)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 2 avg_life med_life 1 54.8 52.9 ``` ::: ::: Notice! how similar this looks to `mutate()` ## Using `summarize()` What if I also wanted to know the **min** and **max** life expectancy? . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder %>% filter(year == 2007) %>% summarize(avg_life = mean(lifeExp), med_life = median(lifeExp), min_life = min(lifeExp), max_life = max(lifeExp)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 avg_life med_life min_life max_life 1 54.8 52.9 39.6 76.4 ``` ::: ::: ## Using `summarize()` What if I also wanted to know the **standard deviation** of life expectancy? . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder %>% filter(year == 2007) %>% summarize(avg_life = mean(lifeExp), med_life = median(lifeExp), min_life = min(lifeExp), max_life = max(lifeExp), sd_life = sd(lifeExp)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 avg_life med_life min_life max_life sd_life 1 54.8 52.9 39.6 76.4 9.63 ``` ::: ::: ## Using `summarize()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder %>% filter(year == 2007) %>% summarize(avg_life = mean(lifeExp), med_life = median(lifeExp), min_life = min(lifeExp), max_life = max(lifeExp), sd_life = sd(lifeExp)) ``` ::: . . . `summarize()` is like `mutate()` in that you are creating *new variables* . . . So note that you have to *name* the new variables! ## We can use summary functions in filter which country had the lowest life expectancy in 2007? . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder %>% filter(year == 2007) %>% filter(lifeExp == min(lifeExp)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Swaziland Africa 2007 39.6 1133066 4513. ``` ::: ::: ## We can use summary functions in filter which countries had above average GPD but below average health? . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gapminder %>% filter(year == 2007) %>% filter(gdpPercap > mean(gdpPercap), lifeExp < mean(lifeExp)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 6 country continent year lifeExp pop gdpPercap 1 Angola Africa 2007 42.7 12420476 4797. 2 Botswana Africa 2007 50.7 1639131 12570. 3 Equatorial Guinea Africa 2007 51.6 551201 12154. 4 Namibia Africa 2007 52.9 2055080 4811. 5 South Africa Africa 2007 49.3 43997828 9270. 6 Swaziland Africa 2007 39.6 1133066 4513. ``` ::: ::: ## Woe unto us: missing data . . . In life, sometimes data is **missing** . . . respondent doesn't answer a question, no one knows Afghanistan's GDP in 1943, etc. . . . R represents missing data as **NA** . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |name |type1 |type2 | height_m| weight_kg| |:--------|:-------|:------|--------:|---------:| |Muk |poison |poison | NA| NA| |Lycanroc |rock |NA | NA| NA| |Hoopa |psychic |ghost | NA| NA| |Golem |rock |ground | NA| NA| |Graveler |rock |ground | NA| NA| |Meowth |normal |dark | NA| NA| ::: ::: ## Summarizing with missing data If you try to *summarize* data that has missing values, R will return `NA`: . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pokemon %>% summarise(average_height = mean(height_m)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 average_height 1 NA ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: callout-note Any math operation with `NA` will return `NA` (.e.g, 3 + `NA` = `NA`) ::: ## What to do? . . . There are whole classes on what to do with missing data (impute, simulate, model, etc.) . . . In this class we will tell R to ignore missing observations . . . We can do this by adding the `na.rm = TRUE` argument to summary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pokemon %>% summarise(average_height = mean(height_m, na.rm = TRUE)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 average_height 1 1.16 ``` ::: ::: ## Remember... . . . If you're trying to calculate a summary statistic and keep getting `NA`... . . . 99.99999% of the time you need to add `na.rm = TRUE` to your function! . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pokemon %>% summarise(average_height = mean(height_m, na.rm = TRUE)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 average_height 1 1.16 ``` ::: ::: ## 🚨 Your turn: 🦁 Animals 🦁 🚨 Using the `msleep` dataset in `tidyverse`: 1. Subset the data to `carni` animals (column name is `vore`) only, make a new variable for the difference in the `sleep_total` and `sleep_rem` as a percent called `rem_perc`. 2. What is the the average percent of `rem_sleep` grouped by the `order`. 3. Using a bar plot, plot the different percentages of rem sleep by order. ::: callout-tip 1. Remember to attach your libraries using `library()` 2. To group by a variable(s) use the function `group_by()` `data |>` `group_by(variable_name) |>` `mutate() or summarize()` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## 🚨 🦁 Animals Answer 🦁 🚨 {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) dat <- msleep |> filter(vore == "carni") |> mutate( rem_perc = sleep_rem/sleep_total * 100 ) dat_2 <- dat |> group_by(order) |> summarize(mean = mean(rem_perc, na.rm = TRUE) ) ggplot(dat_2, aes(y = order, x = mean)) + geom_col(fill = "skyblue") + labs(title = "Average Perct. of REM Sleep for Carnivores by Animal Order", x = "Average Perct. of REM Sleep", y = "Animal Order") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-4_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-35-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## 🚨 🦁 Animals Adv. Answer 🦁 🚨 {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) dat <- msleep |> filter(vore == "carni") |> mutate( rem_perc = sleep_rem/sleep_total * 100 ) |> group_by(order) |> summarize(mean = mean(rem_perc, na.rm = TRUE) ) |> filter(!is.na(mean)) savannah_apex <- c("#D4A373", "#E9D8A6", "#BB3E03", "#94D2BD", "#0A9396") ggplot(dat, aes(x = mean, y = reorder(order, mean), fill=order)) + geom_col() + scale_fill_manual(values = savannah_apex, name = "Animal Order") + labs(title = "Average Perct. of REM Sleep for Carnivores by Animal Order", x = "Average Perct. of REM Sleep", y = "Animal Order") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-4_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-36-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ##

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
